@augusdn - one P2 issue to address before merge, reviewed at `c8182a45428610177b75097eca3ef405cc43ca6d`.

**[P2] Refresh the core inventory after the LOGGER readiness wait** ([tests/conftest.py:3370-3375](https://github.com/sonic-net/sonic-mgmt/blob/c8182a45428610177b75097eca3ef405cc43ca6d/tests/conftest.py#L3370-L3375)).

`collect_after_test()` captures `/var/core` and computes `new_core_dumps` before the new 120-second readiness window, but polling refreshes only `cur_running_config`. If a service crashes during that window and then restarts and recreates the expected LOGGER rows, configuration comparison can succeed while the subsequent core check still uses the earlier, empty inventory. The fixture reports overall success without detecting or collecting the new core. The following module can then treat that file as preexisting.

I reproduced this with the exact fixture and `wait_until` functions in an isolated harness: a core appears after ten simulated seconds, the LOGGER row returns, and the head reports success without fetching the core. The next-module control also passes with that core in its baseline. This is controlled evidence of the added wait's blind window, not a claim that this crash occurred in the hardware acceptance run.

**Suggested fix:** after readiness polling finishes, refresh the core inventory on every DUT and compare it against the original pre-test inventory before the final health verdict. Preserve any already-detected cores and the existing legacy exclusions. Add an integration-level regression case where a core appears during polling but LOGGER restoration subsequently succeeds.

The bounded LOGGER wait itself is reasonable; this change should keep the combined core/config health check covering the same observation window.

Addressed all three review comments:

- Fallback through candidate passwords: now reads a combined "password
  re-prompt or prompt terminator" pattern after each 'enable' attempt
  instead of a fixed '#' pattern, so a wrong-password re-prompt is
  detected and the next candidate is actually tried, rather than being
  lost to a timeout.
- '[confirm]'/'[OK]' matching: patterns are now regex-escaped
  (\[confirm\]/\[OK\]), and the response is checked against the expected
  pattern before treating 'clear line' as successful; a mismatch now
  raises an exception instead of silently logging success.
- Enable secret source: added an optional enable_passwd key per console
  type (alongside the existing user/passwd keys), read from inventory
  and threaded through create_duthost_console() to
  duthost_clear_console_port(). If not configured, elevation is skipped
  with a warning rather than guessing a password.

Validated against a physical Cisco IOS console/terminal server with
enable_passwd configured.

**2. bgpmon refreshes every ~15s, not ~60s**

The [new comment](https://github.com/sonic-net/sonic-mgmt/blob/b5982e76b1455d17de24370b90c5387e4938cee8/tests/common/helpers/bgp.py#L165-L167), the commit message and the PR description say bgpmon polls FRR on a ~60s cycle. As far as I can tell, bgpmon's main loop is [`time.sleep(15)`](https://github.com/sonic-net/sonic-buildimage/blob/ad5af67060b35d460f45541f1e7159f22676a7d9/src/sonic-bgpcfgd/bgpmon/bgpmon.py#L203), and it's the same on master and on the release branches I checked (202305 through 202605). Its `frr.log` activity check shouldn't stretch this either: SONiC [removes FRR's `frr.log` rsyslog outchannel](https://github.com/sonic-net/sonic-buildimage/blob/ad5af67060b35d460f45541f1e7159f22676a7d9/src/sonic-frr/patch/0004-SONiC-ONLY-frr-remove-frr-log-outchannel-to-var-log-frr.log.patch), so `os.stat()` normally fails and [`bgp_activity_detected()`](https://github.com/sonic-net/sonic-buildimage/blob/ad5af67060b35d460f45541f1e7159f22676a7d9/src/sonic-bgpcfgd/bgpmon/bgpmon.py#L59-L68) returns `True` on every loop.

```python
# bgpmon clears NEIGH_STATE_TABLE when the bgp container (re)starts and refreshes
# it every ~15s, so right after a BGP restart / config reload the STATE_DB entry
# can lag behind FRR. Poll STATE_DB until it catches up.
```

### T2 Elastictest failure — root cause (fix-ordering)

The T2 check fails on teardown LogAnalyzer, all matches being the same fpmsyncd error:

```
ERR bgpN#fpmsyncd: sendMsg: zmq send failed, endpoint: tcp://localhost:810x, zmqerrno: 11 (EAGAIN)
```

**Why:** this PR enables the route-perf ZMQ **producer** (fpmsyncd) end-to-end via `SYSTEM_DEFAULTS|swss_zmq`. The orchagent route-ZMQ **consumer** is present in the baseline image (knob consolidation landed in [sonic-swss#4630](https://github.com/sonic-net/sonic-swss/pull/4630)) but is still **single-threaded and not burst-coalesced**. When teardown runs a full `config reload`, the whole route table is reprogrammed in one burst; the consumer can't drain it, the ZMQ send buffer hits its high-water mark, and fpmsyncd's `sendMsg` retries (~40s) then throws. On that throw the update is neither queued nor persisted and is not replayed — so it is a real dropped route, not benign log noise. (The test *cases* pass because the drop occurs at teardown, after all assertions.)

The mechanism is platform-independent — same producer/consumer code path on real HW T2 — so this is not a KVM/vs-only artifact and shouldn't be masked with a LogAnalyzer ignore or a vs-only gate.

**In-flight consumer redesign that resolves it (burst-coalesced route ingress):**
- HLD: [SONiC#2328 — orchagent route programming resiliency](https://github.com/sonic-net/SONiC/pull/2328)
- [sonic-swss-common#1187 — ZmqRouteServer/ZmqRouteConsumerStateTable, burst-coalesced route ingress](https://github.com/sonic-net/sonic-swss-common/pull/1187)
- [sonic-swss#4564 — orchagent ZmqRouteServer for concurrent route updates](https://github.com/sonic-net/sonic-swss/pull/4564)
- [sonic-swss#4563 — orchagent per-Executor task-timing instrumentation](https://github.com/sonic-net/sonic-swss/pull/4563)
- [sonic-utilities#4536 — `show/clear orchagent tasks` (per-Executor timing + scheduling latency)](https://github.com/sonic-net/sonic-utilities/pull/4536)

After analyzing the gap between the headroom calculator and system measurements, BRCM architects confirmed that the calculator is intended as an initial estimator and that the observed differences fall within the expected margin for this type of model. As discussed, the remaining gap is influenced by several interacting real-world factors, including peer PFC response time, cable and transceiver latency, internal latency, and burst dynamics. Because these variables are highly dependent on the specific deployment and continuously interact with one another, developing a theoretical model that accurately captures all scenarios is not practical.

Given these limitations, we are shifting our focus away from theoretical calculations and toward empirical measurements. We are **retiring the theoretical calculator** and planning standalone testing to **capture actual headroom watermarks across a range of port speeds and traffic profiles.** The results, along with a recommended test methodology, are planned for publication in a KB article by Sept end. Our goal is to provide customers with practical guidance based on measured system behavior rather than simplified theoretical assumptions.

We believe this approach will provide more meaningful and actionable data for system vendors and operators and will help establish realistic expectations for headroom requirements across different deployment scenarios.

NextHop agrees with this direction and believes the planned testing will be valuable. As an enhancement, they suggest the following -

1. ASIC data transmitter PFC response time
2. ASIC data receiver headroom (derived either theoretically or empirically), given:
  a) Port speed
  b) PFC response delay at this (data receiver) ASIC input
  c) Traffic profile (MTU, packet size distribution, etc)

If this is done for all ASICs, we system vendors can compute the PFC response delay at data receiver ASIC input (based on transceivers, cable type/length and peer ASIC PFC response delay) and use your model to calculate the headroom. And if this is done for all ASICs, we can find the headroom requirement for different peers e.g. TH6 and Q3d.
